It's been a banner year for Dell Technologies (DELL +3.84%), with its stock up nearly 325% at the time of this writing.
Like many other large tech stocks, it has found its place in the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain, specifically with its AI servers, which have been in high demand this year as graphics processing unit (GPU) clusters and data centers scale.
As such, Dell has been able to distribute more capital back to shareholders, noticeably raising its quarterly dividend by 20% earlier this year. Dell only initiated its dividend program in 2023.

While GPUs and other chips have been at the center of the AI trade, they need to interact with other components in a data center to obtain the capabilities needed to respond to queries from, say, a large language model.
Dell's AI-optimized servers integrate the chips, memory, and other necessary components that power them, including liquid cooling and data storage, into a full server and rack.
The company also performs quality control and then ships them to customers such as neoclouds and other large customers, including hyperscalers that operate their own data centers.
While Dell isn't the only company building and selling full-scale AI racks, it's been all hands on deck amid massive AI demand, resulting in shortages across the supply chain.

Dell Technologies (NYSE:DELL) joined a planned $15b AI data center initiative in Japan focused on power hungry AI infrastructure.
The Japanese project is intended to support large scale AI workloads by pairing new data facilities with dedicated power supply capacity.
Dell also introduced rugged laptops with on device AI features and added security aimed at field and mission critical use cases.

3 things going right for Dell Technologies that this headline doesn't cover.
Dell Technologies doubles down on AI infrastructure while testing new edges
The Dell Technologies Narrative revolves around turning a huge AI infrastructure backlog into earnings, while leaning on higher margin storage and services rather than old-style PC cycles. This Japan data center partnership and the rugged, AI-enabled laptops plug straight into that story by tying Dell gear more tightly to power hungry enterprise workloads and edge environments.
"Dell Technologies is experiencing accelerating demand for AI servers and data center solutions as enterprises globally increase investments in AI and machine learning workloads and digital transformation...

The Japan project speaks directly to that AI server and storage thesis. It puts Dell infrastructure next to dependable power supply at large scale, which fits the Narrative's focus on converting a US$95b AI backlog and a large pipeline into deployed systems. This leans toward the reward side of the story that links enterprise AI demand and a richer product mix to potential future earnings power.

They push AI closer to field workers in sectors such as public safety and energy, and that can feed back into demand for storage, services and support.
